target_customer: Developers and teams who needed a lightweight real-time shared text and code editor, including companies running remote coding interviews
problem: After Etherpad was shut down, people lacked a fast simple way to edit text and code together in real time, and Google Docs was not suited to code.
business_model: Free web app at launch; no monetization described in sources, later absorbed into Salesforce
product_category: Real-time collaborative text and code editor

founders.name: Jason Chen
founders.background_notes: YC page says he later founded Slab and leads the open source Quill editor.

founders.name: Byron Milligan
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page; no bio there.

competitors.name: Etherpad
competitors.what: Real-time collaborative editor from YC alum AppJet
competitors.traction_then: Google acquired it in December 2009 and it was later open sourced; its servers were shut down

competitors.name: Google Docs
competitors.traction_then: large user base; the Stypi cofounder argued it was heavier and not suited to code

technical_complexity.rationale: Real-time operational transformation editing with a lightweight browser client, built from scratch without reusing Etherpad code, plus syntax highlighting. Conflict free merging is the hard part but was well understood.

defensibility.rationale: A free single feature tool with Google Docs and open source Etherpad forks as substitutes and no lock in; the value was the team and its real-time technology.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Google already offered real-time editing in Docs. Salesforce acquired Stypi in May 2012; TheNextWeb said it was unclear whether this was an acquihire or full acquisition, and the YC page says the team kept building real-time technology there.

market_need_then: Etherpad's shutdown had left a gap for fast collaborative editing, and TechCrunch described Stypi as Etherpad reborn at launch in August 2011. The YC page says Apple, Pinterest and Palantir used it in remote interviews.

branding.domain_note: Used stypi.com; it returned HTTP 503 at fetch time.

identity.voice_and_tone: Minimal, lightweight positioning versus Google Docs

branding.community_and_virality: Press coverage at launch (TechCrunch, Korben, blogs) and use in interviews; no merch or fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Known among developers for interview use and covered at launch, but a hard to spell invented name and no sourced evidence of a lasting identity.

pivots.to: Collaborative code editor used for remote interviews
pivots.why: YC page says the first product was a collaborative code editor; the launch coverage showed programmer features were added because coders were a main Etherpad use case

outcome_analysis: Stypi was a two person team that rebuilt Etherpad style real-time editing for developers and gained use in company interview processes. Salesforce acquired it in May 2012, about nine months after launch, with undisclosed terms, and the YC page says the team kept building real-time technology there, which points to a team and technology acquisition rather than a standalone product outcome.
notes: Company website stypi.com returned HTTP 503. No funding amounts found; CB Insights lists a single round tied to the acquisition (aggregator, not recorded). Mergr lists the deal on May 1, 2012; press dated May 2, 2012; recorded as 2012-05. The acquihire factor is supported only by TheNextWeb saying it was unclear whether the deal was an acquihire. TechCrunch's July 2012 article on the mechanics of a small acquisition was seen only as a search result title and not confirmed to be about Stypi. Education and prior employers not found. The pivot entry is a loose characterization, not a dated change.
